papers.title_in_file: Noise-Resilient Single-Pixel Compressive Sensing with Single Photon Counting
papers.version_note: Research Square preprint (posted 10 Oct 2023, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3349937/v1). The cover page says a version was published in Communications Physics in March 2024. The supplementary file (Table S1, S2, Figures S10, S11) is only listed on the last page and is not in this file.
papers.not_read: The supplementary PDF (Tables S1 and S2, Figures S10 and S11) is only listed on p.11 and is not part of this file, so it was not read.

figures.shows: Experimental layout: mode-locked laser split by WDMs into probe (about 1554.3 nm) and pump (about 1564.3 nm) arms with EDFAs. The probe goes through an attenuator and a 99:1 beamsplitter to a DMD (Walsh 2D patterns) and an SLM (MNIST digits), through 4-f relay lenses. A 50:50 fibre beamsplitter then feeds an InGaAs SPD (direct detection) and a PPLN module with pump, followed by a Si SPD (QPMS), both read by a time tagger. A separate EDFA/WDM branch injects ASE noise. Insets (a) to (e) are normalized spectra, in dB against wavelength in nm, of the probe, pump, ASE, filtered ASE noise and the upconverted output near 780 nm.
figures.confirmed_by: The experimental setup is sketched in Fig. 1.

figures.shows: (a) Raw DD photon counts (y up to about 150) against event index (x, 0 to about 800, i.e. 80 patterns). (b) Raw QPMS photon counts (y up to about 400) against event index (x, 0 to about 2000). (c) Mean photon counts per DMD pattern (y up to about 200) against pattern index (x, 0 to 300). (d) Neural network diagram: 300 input values, 7 layers in total, 10 output nodes for digits 0 to 9.
figures.confirmed_by: which extract 300 features from each digit image.

figures.shows: Four normalized 10x10 confusion matrices (real label against predicted label, colour scale 0 to 1). (a) DD, 600 µs per mask, 398.6 average counts, ~14 nW, 82.8% accuracy. (b) DD, 800 µs, 551.2 counts, ~14 nW, 90%. (c) DD, 800 µs, 391.5 counts, ~8.5 nW, 80.4%. (d) QPMS, 200 µs, 485.8 counts, ~14 nW, 98%.
figures.confirmed_by: As an example, Fig. 3 shows the confusion matrices for both DD and QPMS under different integration times and different probe powers.

figures.shows: Background (dark) photon counts (y, 0 to about 30) against SPD integration time (x, 0 to 100 µs). Red triangles are the InGaAs SPD with probe and pump off, rising to about 29 counts at about 100 µs. Green diamonds are the QPMS channel with pump power 16.5 dBm, reaching about 8 counts at about 40 µs. Both follow smooth fit curves that look nearly linear, though the caption calls them quadratic.
figures.confirmed_by: To check this, Fig. 4 plots the measured dark counts of the two detection channels.

figures.shows: Classification accuracy (y, about 20 to 100%) against average photon counts per mask (x, 0 to about 2000). Five curves: QPMS with 300, 100 and 40 masks, and DD with 300 and 100 masks. The QPMS curves are at about 90 to 99% across the range. The DD curves rise from about 26 to 42% at the lowest counts to about 82 to 90% near 550 counts, where they end.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 5 summarizes the classiﬁcation accuracy as a function of the average detected photon number per DMD mask, for both detection channels and different number of DMD masks used.

figures.shows: Classification accuracy (y, about 20 to 100%) against ASE-noise SNR (x, about -30 to 10 dB). QPMS with 300 masks and with 100 masks run from about -27 dB to about 3 dB. They are near 98 to 99% above about -23 dB, and about 94% (300 masks) and about 88% (100 masks) at about -27 dB. DD curves exist only at about 0 dB and about 3 dB, rising from about 21 to 22% to about 52% (300 masks) and about 39% (100 masks).
figures.confirmed_by: The results are shown in Fig. 6.

figures.shows: Two normalized 10x10 confusion matrices for QPMS detection, 300 masks. (a) Trained at SNR 0 dB, tested without noise. (b) Trained at SNR -10 dB, tested at SNR -17 dB. Diagonal entries are 0.92 to 1 in both; the off-diagonal entries printed are at most 0.08.
figures.confirmed_by: In both cases, the classiﬁcation accuracy remains rather high, no less than 98% with 300 masks.

papers.what_it_is: An experimental preprint on single-pixel compressive sensing with Walsh patterns and a neural-network MNIST classifier. It compares direct InGaAs single-photon detection with quantum parametric mode sorting (QPMS) upconversion detection under dark-count and injected in-band ASE noise.

assertions.value: The authors report 94% classification accuracy with QPMS detection when the in-band noise is 500 times stronger than the received signal.
quotes: We achieve 94% classiﬁcation accuracy in the presence of 500 times stronger in-band noise than the signal received.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experiment on 1000 MNIST samples.
assertions.reader_inference: One 75/25 train/test split of 1000 images; no repeated runs or error bars are reported.

assertions.value: The authors use a total of 1000 MNIST handwritten digits as targets (100 images per digit), with 75% for training and 25% for testing. Each is sampled by 40, 100, or 300 Walsh 2D patterns, with compression ratios of 0.07%, 0.17%, or 0.52%.
quotes: we use a total of 1000 MNIST handwritten digits as our targets, with 75% for training and 25% for testing, each sampled by 40, 100, or 300 Walsh 2D patterns
corresponding to a compression ratio of 0.07%, 0.17%, or 0.52%, respectively
In our experiment, there are 100 different images for each digit from the MNIST dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the dataset and split as their own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The dataset is small (1000 samples, 250 tests), so accuracy values are coarse (steps of 0.4%).

assertions.value: The authors state that the classifier is a deep neural network with 7 layers in total (input layer, five hidden layers, output layer). ReLU activations are applied to the hidden layers and a log-softmax function is used between the second last and the last layer.
quotes: The DNN consists of a total of 7 layers including the input layer, ﬁve hidden layers, and the output layer.
ReLU activation functions are applied to the hidden layers
while a log-softmax function is used between the second last layer and the last layer
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own classifier architecture.
assertions.reader_inference: The classifier is purely classical and runs on measured photon counts; no quantum processing of the data is involved.

assertions.value: The authors state that for DD each event counts photons for 100 µs with 10 events per DMD pattern, of which 8 are averaged. For QPMS each event counts for 40 µs with 25 events per pattern, of which 20 are averaged. The effective integration time of photon counting is 0.8 millisecond in the QPMS example case.
quotes: where each event counts photons for 100 µs, and there are 10 events for each DMD pattern
where each event counts photons for 40 µs, and there are 25 events for each DMD pattern
by averaging over 20 of the 25 events
by averaging over 8 of the 10 events
The effective integration time of photon counting is thus 0.8 millisecond in this case.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the paper's description of its own data acquisition.
assertions.reader_inference: The per-event times (15 to 100 µs for DD, 3 to 40 µs for QPMS) quoted in the introduction are not the per-mask integration times (such as 600 or 800 µs) quoted in the results.

assertions.value: The authors state that the femtosecond mode-locked laser is at about 1550 nm with a 50 MHz repetition rate. The probe is a 6 ps pulse centred at 1554.3 nm and the pump a 6 ps pulse centred at 1564.3 nm. The upconverted output is at a wavelength of 779.59 nm. The SLM displays the MNIST digits as binary phase patterns of 0 or 3π/8, resized to 240×240.
quotes: operating at a repetition rate of 50 MHz
6 ps probe pulse centered at 1554.3 nm
the 6 ps pump pulse centered at 1564.3 nm
operating at a wavelength of 779.59 nm
Each pixel in the phase patterns is expressed as a binary phase value of either 0 or 3π/8.
we resize them to 240×240 images
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental configuration.

assertions.value: The authors state a total detection efficiency of 4.2% for the DD channel (InGaAs SPD with quantum efficiency set to 20% and a 1 ns effective gate width) and 12.0% for the QPMS channel. The Si-SPD in the QPMS channel has a quantum efficiency of 66%.
quotes: InGaAs-SPD is set to be 20%
4.2% for the DD channel.
the total detection efﬁciency for the QPMS channel is 12.0%.
the Si-SPD has a quantum efﬁciency of 66%
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors as the configuration of their own detectors.
assertions.reader_inference: The DD and QPMS channels differ in efficiency, dark counts and saturation, so differences in accuracy are not attributable to mode filtering alone.

assertions.value: The authors report that DD classification accuracy rises with average photon counts per mask. It is 82.8% at 398.6 counts (600 µs per mask, ~14 nW) and 90% at 551.2 counts (800 µs, ~14 nW). At 800 µs it is 80.4% at 391.5 counts (~8.5 nW) and only 31.6% at 299.7 counts (~4 nW).
quotes: the average photon counts per mask is 398.6, which gives an 82.8% classiﬁcation accuracy
the average photon count per mask becomes 551.2, and the classiﬁcation accuracy improves to 90%
the average photon counts per mask is 391.5, and the classiﬁcation accuracy drops to 80.4%
the average photon counts is 299.7, for which the classiﬁcation accuracy is only 31.6%
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical results from single runs on 1000 samples.
assertions.reader_inference: Each accuracy comes from one training run on 250 test images.

assertions.value: The authors report that QPMS detection with a 200 µs integration time and ~14 nW probe power gives 485.8 average photon counts per DMD mask and 98% classification accuracy. They state this is significantly higher than DD with similar or even higher photon counts.
quotes: With an integration time of 200 µs and probe power of ∼14 nW, the average photon count per DMD mask is 485.8.
The classiﬁcation accuracy in this case is 98%, which is signiﬁcantly higher than the DD case with similar or even higher photon counts.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical single-configuration result.
assertions.reader_inference: The two channels have different efficiencies and integration times, so the comparison is at matched photon counts, not matched hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report dark counts of about 0.29 per 10 microsecond integration time for DD and about 0.21 per 10 µs for QPMS. They translate to 234 per 800 µs for DD, about half the average photon count, versus 40 per 200 µs for QPMS, about 8.2% of the average count.
quotes: 0.29 per 10 microsecond integration time for DD, and about 0.21 per 10 µs for QPMS.
They translate to 234 per 800 µs integration time for the DD channel in Fig. 3(b), which is about half of the average photon count.
the dark count is only 40 per 200 µs integration time for the QPMS channel in Fig. 3(d), about 8.2% of the average count.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured dark counts from the authors' detectors.
assertions.reader_inference: The quoted rates look off by a factor of 10: 234 per 800 µs implies about 0.29 per µs, and Figure 4 shows about 29 counts at 100 µs. The 'per 10 µs' wording is probably a typo.

assertions.value: The authors attribute the much better QPMS performance over DD in the confusion-matrix comparison mainly to its much lower dark counts.
quotes: The much better performance in QPMS over DD as seen in Fig. 3 is mainly attributed to its much lower dark counts.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' interpretation supported by measured dark counts; no control that isolates dark counts.
assertions.reader_inference: Efficiency also differs (12.0% vs 4.2%), and the paper cites this too, so the dark-count attribution is not isolated.

assertions.value: The authors report that at 119.7 average photon counts per mask QPMS accuracy is 97.2% with 300 masks and 93.2% with 100 masks. It then quickly saturates to 99.2% for both cases at around 500 average photon counts.
quotes: For QPMS, when the average photon number is 119.7 per mask, the accuracy is 97.2% with 300 masks and 93.2% with 100 masks.
quickly saturates to 99.2% for both cases, when the average photon count increases to around 500
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one set of runs.

assertions.value: The authors report that for DD at 59.5 average photon counts the accuracy is 42.4% with 300 masks and only 26.4% with 100 masks. At about 550 average counts it rises to around 90% and 82.8% respectively, still much lower than QPMS.
quotes: For example, with 59.5 average photon count, it is 42.4% with 300 masks and only 26.4% with 100 masks.
As the average count increases to 550, the accuracy increases to around 90% and 82.8%, respectively, for the two mask numbers
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one set of runs.

assertions.value: The authors state that, due to InGaAs-SPD saturation, the average photon count cannot be increased further for the DD channel, which limits the DD comparison to about 550 average counts.
quotes: Due to the InGaAs-SPD saturation, the average photon count cannot be further increased for the DD channel.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their DD measurements.
assertions.reader_inference: DD accuracy beyond about 550 counts per mask was not measured, so the DD/QPMS gap at high counts is untested.

assertions.value: The authors state that the InGaAs SPD dark count can be reduced to only 0.01 per 10 microsecond by setting quantum efficiency to 15%, but the saturation counts are then lowered by more than a half, reducing the dynamic range of detected signal photons.
quotes: the dark count for the InGaAs SPD can be reduced to only 0.01 per 10 microsecond by setting quantum efﬁciency to 15%
the saturation counts will be lowered by more than a half, so that the dynamic range of detected signal photons is reduced
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated detector behaviour without data shown in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Si-SPD, compared with the InGaAs SPD, has orders of magnitude lower dark counts, at least 10 times higher saturation counts and several times higher efficiency. They call this a practical advantage of QPMS as an upconversion single photon detector.
quotes: with orders of magnitude lower dark counts, at least 10 times higher saturation counts, and several times higher efﬁciency
This is a practical advantage of QPMS as an upconversion single photon detector.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' comparison; no numerical data for the Si-SPD saturation are shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The 'orders of magnitude lower dark counts' sits oddly with the measured per-40 µs counts (11.8 vs 8.5) given later, which are similar.

assertions.value: The authors define the SNR as 10 log10 of (Noff − Ndark)/(Ntot − Noff). Noff is the photon count without ASE, Ndark the same count with the probe shut off, and Ntot the same count with the added ASE noise. Counts are taken on the InGaAs SPD for the first image of digit 1 with the 31st Walsh pattern on the DMD.
quotes: the signal to noise ratio (SNR), is deﬁned as 10 log10 [(Noff − Ndark)/(Ntot − Noff)]
Here Noff is the photon counts without ASE
Ndarkis the same photon counts but with the probe shut off.
Ntot is the same photon counts but with the added ASE noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its SNR measure.
assertions.reader_inference: SNR is referenced to one pattern/image (the highest-count combination), not an average over all masks.

assertions.value: The authors report that for DD with probe power about 8.5 nW and ASE equal to the probe (SNR 0 dB), classification accuracy is only 22.0% (300 masks, 300 training epochs). Halving the ASE power gives SNR 3 dB and 51.6% accuracy. When the ASE is doubled to reach SNR -3 dB, the SPD saturates.
quotes: For DD, the probe power after the FC1 is set to be about 8.5 nW.
The classiﬁcation accuracy is only 22.0% after 300 training epoches with 300 masks on the DMD.
Halving the ASE power increases the SNR to 3 dB and improves the accuracy to 51.6%.
As we attempt to double the ASE to reduce the SNR to -3 dB, the SPD saturates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical single-run results.
assertions.reader_inference: DD could be tested at only two SNR points (0 and 3 dB) because of saturation. The introduction quotes the no-noise DD baseline as 80.2%, while the results give 80.4%.

assertions.value: The authors report that QPMS classification accuracy remains above 98% when the signal is down to 100 times weaker than the noise.
quotes: the classiﬁcation accuracy remains above 98% when the signal is down to 100 times weaker than the noise
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical single-experiment result.
assertions.reader_inference: The ASE noise is an injected in-band proxy for ambient light, not real sunlight or scene background.

assertions.value: The authors report that at SNR -27 dB, where the signal is 500 times weaker than the noise, QPMS classification accuracy is still 94%. They attribute the weak probe to attenuating it to around 6 nW with the Si SPD.
quotes: Even when SNR is -27 dB, for which the signal is 500 times weaker, the classiﬁcation accuracy is still 94%.
we are able to attenuate the prob power to around ∼6 nW so that the SNR
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical single-run result.
assertions.reader_inference: -27 dB is the lowest SNR measured, so no failure point for QPMS was found.

assertions.value: The authors state that in their experiment QPMS rejects over 99.9% of noise, citing earlier work, so that the detected noise at the Si-SPD is only at the dark count level, much weaker than the signal.
quotes: QPMS rejects over 99.9% of noise
so that the actual detected noise by the Si-SPD is only on the dark count level, much weaker than the signal
assertions.certainty_reason: The rejection figure is attributed to a cited prior work and no measurement of it is shown here.

assertions.value: The authors define the noise equivalence of dark counts (NEDC) as the detector dark count divided by the total detection efficiency.
quotes: deﬁned as the detector dark count divided by the total detection efﬁciency
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the NEDC measure.

assertions.value: The authors report that for DD, per 40 µs, the dark count is 11.8 and the efficiency 4.2%, giving a NEDC of 281. For QPMS the dark count is 8.5 per 40 µs and the efficiency 12.0%, giving a NEDC of 71.
quotes: For DD, per 40 µs, the dark count is 11.8 and the efﬁciency is 4.2%, so that the NEDC is 281.
For QPMS, the dark count is 8.5 per 40 µs and the efﬁciency is 12.0%, which gives a NEDC of 71.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values computed from measured dark counts and stated efficiencies.
assertions.reader_inference: 11.8/0.042 is about 281 and 8.5/0.12 is about 71, so the arithmetic checks. The raw dark counts per 40 µs are similar; the NEDC gap comes mostly from efficiency.

assertions.value: The authors report that training QPMS on one ASE noise level and testing on another (train 0 dB SNR, test without noise; train -10 dB, test -17 dB) keeps classification accuracy no less than 98% with 300 masks.
quotes: we perform training on one ASE noise level and testing on a different level
In both cases, the classiﬁcation accuracy remains rather high, no less than 98% with 300 masks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Two empirical train/test noise configurations from one experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: Only two mismatch cases were run.

assertions.value: The authors suggest that the high timing resolution of QPMS (about 10 ps) might let photon counts carry relative pixel distribution information, and state they have not been able to verify this in the study.
quotes: it approaches that of QPMS (about 10 ps)
However, we have not been able to verify it yet in this study.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors explicitly state the hypothesis is not verified.
assertions.reader_inference: The time-of-flight explanation for the QPMS advantage remains speculative.

assertions.value: The authors report that with 100 instead of 300 Walsh 2D patterns, DD accuracy decreases by about 10%, while no obvious change happens to QPMS detection.
quotes: We also try to sample targets with 100 Walsh 2D patterns
The classiﬁcation accuracy of DD decreases for ∼10% compared with sample targets with 300 Walsh 2D patterns
but no obvious change happens to QPMS detection with the
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical summary in the introduction; figures show some variation.
assertions.reader_inference: Figure 5 shows QPMS 100-mask accuracy about 4 points lower at the lowest counts (93.2% vs 97.2%), so 'no obvious change' holds only at higher counts.

assertions.value: The authors state that with ASE noise there is no notable change in QPMS detection when the SNR level is larger than -20dB, while about a 30% change happens to the DD when the SNR level is 3dB.
quotes: no notable change happens to QPMS detection when the SNR level is larger than -20dB, while ∼30% happens to the DD when the SNR level is 3dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: Summary statement whose reference quantity is not fully specified.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence is ambiguous about what changes by about 30% (probably the 100-mask versus 300-mask DD gap or the drop from the no-noise baseline).

assertions.value: The authors report that for DD the classification accuracy drops significantly when the mean photon numbers fall below 300.
quotes: Our results ﬁnd that for DD, the accuracy drops signiﬁcantly when the mean photon numbers fall below 300.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result summarized in the introduction.
assertions.reader_inference: This is consistent with the DD data point of 31.6% at 299.7 counts.

assertions.value: The authors report that without ASE noise DD accuracy is 80.4% with 300 masks (probe power ~8.5 nW, dark counts ~234), falling to 41.2% at ~6 nW and 31.6% at ~4 nW.
quotes: the classiﬁcation accuracy for DD is 80.4% with 300 masks after 300 epochs of training
the classiﬁcation accuracy drops to 41.2% with the probe power ∼6 nW, and to 31.6% with the probe power ∼4 nW
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical single-run results.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that by rejecting noise while improving detection efficiency, QPMS allows highly accurate classification of MNIST images even when the signal is mixed with orders of magnitude stronger in-band noise.
quotes: By rejecting the noise while improving the detection efﬁciency, it allows highly accurate classiﬁcation of MNIST images even the signal is mixed with orders of magnitude stronger in-band noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' conclusion from one MNIST experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The scope is MNIST classification with injected ASE noise at 1554 nm; applications named (astronomy, biomedical diagnosis) are not tested.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 4: the InGaAs-SPD (DD) dark counts rise from about 4 counts at about 15 µs to about 29 counts at about 100 µs, and the QPMS (Si-SPD) counts rise from about 1 count at about 3 µs to about 8 counts at about 40 µs, both close to linear in integration time.
quotes: The background counts versus the integration time on the InGaAs SPD and Si SPD.
To check this, Fig. 4 plots the measured dark counts of the two detection channels.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.
assertions.reader_inference: These rates (about 0.29 per µs for DD, about 0.21 per µs for QPMS) match the stated 234 per 800 µs and 8.5 per 40 µs, so the text's 'per 10 µs' appears to be an error. The caption calls the fits quadratic although they look linear.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 5: QPMS detection with 40 masks reaches about 88 to 91% at low average photon counts (about 100 to 300), then rises to about 98% near about 500 counts and about 99% at higher counts up to about 2000.
quotes: QPMS represented by the green, the red, and the black curves with 200 training epochs
The QPMS encodes the probe optically, which helps us go further in the compressive ratio.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot; the 40-mask result is not stated in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: Forty masks is a compression ratio of about 0.07%, so QPMS keeps near-99% accuracy at very high compression at high counts.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 6: QPMS accuracy with 300 masks is about 94% at about -27 dB and about 98 to 99% from about -23 dB to about 3 dB; with 100 masks it is about 88% at about -27 dB. DD has points only at about 0 dB and about 3 dB, with about 22% and about 52% (300 masks) and about 21% and about 39% (100 masks).
quotes: The classiﬁcation accuracy of DD and QPMS single photon detection vs SNR (dB) of the ASE noise with 100 or 300 input values into the neural network.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.
assertions.reader_inference: The 100-mask QPMS curve degrades more at -27 dB than the 300-mask curve; the DD 100-mask result at 3 dB (about 39%) is about 13 points below the 300-mask result.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 3: in DD at 600 µs per mask, digit 6 is the weakest class, with a diagonal of about 0.52 and about 0.32 predicted as 5. In DD at 800 µs and ~8.5 nW, digit 6 has about 0.56 on the diagonal and digit 8 has about 0.64. The QPMS matrix has diagonals of about 0.92 to about 1.00 for all digits.
quotes: Normalized confusion matrices for DD ((a), (b), and (c)) and QPMS detection ((d))
(d) classiﬁcation accuracy is 98%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Per-class values read from a printed confusion matrix; one run each.
assertions.reader_inference: DD errors concentrate on visually similar digit pairs (5/6, 6/8); the paper does not discuss per-class errors.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 7: for QPMS trained at SNR 0 dB and tested without noise, the diagonal entries are about 0.92 to about 1.00; for training at -10 dB and testing at -17 dB, the diagonal entries are about 0.92 to about 1.00, with the lowest at digit 3 (about 0.92).
quotes: QPMS detection: In this case, the training process involves using a speciﬁc level of ASE noise as the training dataset (200 training epochs), while other levels of ASE noise are used as the testing dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read from a printed confusion matrix.
assertions.reader_inference: The text calls this 'supplementary figure 7' although it appears as Figure 7 in the main body.
